All were measured this session against\n    <code>data-grid-gb</code> and the committed OSM extracts.</p>\n\n  <div class=\"scroll\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th>measured</th><th class=\"r\">value</th><th>consequence for the build</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">route factor, built &divide; straight</td><td class=\"r cy\">median 1.16 &middot; p10 1.03 &middot; p90 1.48</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">The straight line is wrong by +3% to +48%. This is the dominant error term.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">route factor, cable circuits only</td><td class=\"r cy\">1.34 (n=95)</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Cables follow made ground. This is the number a routed engine must reproduce.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">route factor, overhead only</td><td class=\"r cy\">1.13 (n=503)</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Lines go more directly. Road routing must <em>not</em> be applied to OHL.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">connection points with coordinates</td><td class=\"r bad\">502 of 886 &middot; 57%</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Any &ldquo;nearest&rdquo; claim today is nearest-among-57%. Routing cannot fix an absent point.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">400 kV sites unlocatable</td><td class=\"r bad\">141 of 355 &middot; 40%</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Geocoding is a prerequisite, not a nice-to-have.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">colliding normalised site names</td><td class=\"r bad\">34 keys &middot; 69 sites</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">7.5% of sites may bind to the wrong asset. Fix before adding geometry on top.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">road graph available</td><td class=\"r\">294,018 ways &middot; 1,953,165 segments</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Primary + trunk, already committed. Big enough to route, too big to ship raw.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">railway graph available</td><td class=\"r\">89,933 ways &middot; 607,762 segments</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Enough to detect and price every crossing.</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n\n  <div class=\"measured\">\n    <div class=\"lbl\">The finding that sets the priority</div>\n    <p>Choosing between a spherical and an ellipsoidal earth model moves a 15 km answer by roughly\n      <strong>0.1&ndash;0.3%</strong>. The route factor moves it by <strong>3&ndash;48%</strong>. Refining the\n      earth model while quoting a straight line is polishing a rounding error inside a much larger one.\n      The corridor is where the accuracy is.</p>\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">02</span> Where each piece lives</h2>\n  <p>The estate already has a working shape: a maths repo with no data, data repos that pin their\n    sources and publish verified products, and consumers that read products and never sources. This\n    scope keeps that shape rather than inventing one.</p>\n\n<pre><span class=\"c\">  source                          derivation                      consumer</span>\n  NESO ETYS 2025      ─────►  data-grid-gb            ─────►  Atlas cartridge\n  (SHA-256 pinned)            connection-points.v3            substation-intelligence\n                              gb-transmission-network\n\n  OSM roads, rail     ─────►  <span class=\"cy\">data-grid-routes</span>        ─────►  <span class=\"cy\">Atlas cartridge</span>\n  (to be pinned)              <span class=\"cy\">corridor-graph.v1</span>              <span class=\"cy\">corridor-intelligence</span>\n                              <span class=\"cy\">routed-distances.v1</span>\n                                     ▲\n                                     │ uses\n                              <span class=\"cy\">grid-distance-maths</span>\n                              geodesy + <span class=\"cy\">routing kernel</span>\n                              no data, dual implementation</pre>\n\n  <ul>\n    <li><strong>grid-distance-maths</strong> stays the pure kernel &mdash; no network access, no data files,\n      two independent implementations, parity-tested. Gains a routing module and the stress harness.</li>\n    <li><strong>data-grid-routes</strong> is new and follows the <code>data-*</code> convention exactly: fetch\n      OSM extracts, pin by SHA-256, derive products, verify, publish.</li>\n    <li><strong>corridor-intelligence</strong> is a new Atlas cartridge that reads products and computes nothing\n      it can read. It pins a schema and refuses on mismatch, the way substation-intelligence does.</li>\n  </ul>\n  <p>Nothing in <code>data-grid-gb</code> changes. The corridor engine is additive.</p>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">03</span> Module A &mdash; the maths kernel</h2>\n  <p>Pure functions over coordinates. No fetching, no globals, no knowledge of substations. Everything\n    here is testable without a network and runs identically in Node and Python.</p>\n\n  <div class=\"grid2\">\n    <div>\n      <h3>Already present</h3>\n      <ul>\n        <li><code>distanceKm</code>, <code>distanceEllipsoidalKm</code>, <code>pathLengthKm</code></li>\n        <li><code>initialBearingDeg</code>, <code>destinationPoint</code></li>\n        <li><code>distanceToSegmentKm</code>, <code>distanceToLineKm</code></li>\n        <li><code>geodesicCircle</code>, <code>circleApproximationError</code></li>\n        <li><code>polygonAreaKm2</code>, <code>SpatialIndex</code></li>\n      </ul>\n    </div>\n    <div>\n      <h3>To add</h3>\n      <ul>\n        <li><code>snapToGraph(point, graph, maxKm)</code> &mdash; nearest routable node with the snap distance returned, never hidden</li>\n        <li><code>route(a, b, graph, weights)</code> &mdash; A* with an admissible great-circle heuristic</li>\n        <li><code>crossings(path, barriers)</code> &mdash; segment-intersection counts by barrier class</li>\n        <li><code>corridorLength(path)</code> &mdash; geodesic polyline length, not planar</li>\n        <li><code>routeFactor(path, straight)</code> &mdash; the ratio, reported not applied</li>\n        <li><code>simplify(path, toleranceM)</code> &mdash; geodesic-aware Douglas-Peucker</li>\n      </ul>\n    </div>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"measured\">\n    <div class=\"lbl\">Design rule</div>\n    <p>A snap distance is part of the answer. If a substation is 900 m from the nearest routable road,\n      the route is 900 m short at one end and the card must say so. Silently snapping is how a\n      routing engine starts lying.</p>\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">04</span> Module B &mdash; the stress harness</h2>\n  <p>Four independent layers. A geometry bug that survives all four is a bug nobody on this estate\n    could have found by reading.</p>\n\n  <h3>1. Invariants &mdash; property-based, thousands of random cases</h3>\n<pre>identity        d(a,a) = 0\nsymmetry        d(a,b) = d(b,a)                     to 1e-9 relative\ntriangle        d(a,c) &le; d(a,b) + d(b,c)\nbearing round   destination(a, bearing(a,b), d(a,b)) = b\nroute &ge; line    routeKm &ge; straightKm                 always, no exceptions\nroute factor    1.0 &le; factor &le; 10.0                  outside this, fail loudly\npath length     sum of leg lengths = corridorLength(path)\ndeterminism     same input, same output, across both implementations</pre>\n\n  <h3>2. Adversarial cases &mdash; a fixed corpus, not random</h3>\n  <ul>\n    <li>Coincident and near-coincident points (1 mm, 1 cm, 1 m apart)</li>\n    <li>Antipodal and near-antipodal pairs &mdash; where iterative inverse solutions fail to converge</li>\n    <li>The poles, and paths crossing them</li>\n    <li>The antimeridian, in both directions</li>\n    <li>Points either side of the Greenwich meridian and the equator, for sign handling</li>\n    <li>Degenerate graphs: an isolated node, a disconnected component, a zero-length edge</li>\n    <li>A substation with no road within 50 km &mdash; the engine must return <em>no route</em>, not a wrong one</li>\n  </ul>\n\n  <h3>3. Oracles &mdash; independent, external, authoritative</h3>\n  <div class=\"scroll\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th>oracle</th><th>what it proves</th><th>tolerance</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">Karney GeodTest</td><td class=\"d\">Geodesic inverse solutions against 500,000 published high-precision cases</td><td>&lt; 1 mm</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">the second implementation</td><td class=\"d\">JS against Python on identical inputs, neither knowing the other's answers</td><td>1e-9 relative</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">published cable circuits</td><td class=\"d\">Routed distance against NESO's own <code>cable_km</code>, n=95</td><td>see below</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">pandapower</td><td class=\"d\">Electrical quantities only, once the engine computes any. BSD-3, cited not bundled.</td><td>per quantity</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n\n  <h3>4. The acceptance test that matters</h3>\n  <div class=\"measured\">\n    <div class=\"lbl\">Self-validating, using data you already publish</div>\n    <p>NESO publishes <code>cable_km</code> for 95 circuits whose endpoints both have coordinates. Those\n      are real buried cable routes with a known built length. <strong>Route between the two substations\n      along the road graph and compare.</strong> The straight line is wrong by a median of 34% on this set.\n      A routed engine that does not beat that is not earning its complexity.</p>\n    <p><strong>Gate:</strong> median absolute error against published <code>cable_km</code> must fall below\n      <strong>15%</strong>, and the routed estimate must beat the straight line on at least\n      <strong>80%</strong> of the 95 circuits. Published as a report, not asserted.</p>\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">05</span> Module C &mdash; routing, and the railway question</h2>\n\n  <h3>Following roads already solves most of it</h3>\n  <p>A cable route follows made ground because the wayleave, the trenching and the crossings are all\n    cheaper there. Where a road crosses a railway it does so at an existing bridge or culvert &mdash;\n    infrastructure that already has the crossing solved. So <em>route along roads</em> delivers most of\n    <em>avoid railways</em> for free, and it is why the measured cable factor is 1.34 rather than 1.0.</p>\n\n  <h3>Avoidance is the wrong model; cost is the right one</h3>\n  <p>A hard prohibition makes some routes impossible and others absurd &mdash; a project on the far side\n    of a main line has no route at all. Every crossing is a consent event with a cost and a duration, so\n    the correct structure is a weighted graph where a crossing is expensive rather than forbidden. Set the\n    weight high enough and avoidance falls out; set it to infinity and you get a broken engine.</p>\n\n<pre>weight(edge) = lengthKm\n             + <span class=\"cy\">RAIL_PENALTY_KM</span>     &times; railwayCrossings(edge)\n             + <span class=\"cy\">MOTORWAY_PENALTY_KM</span> &times; motorwayCrossings(edge)\n             + <span class=\"cy\">WATER_PENALTY_KM</span>    &times; watercourseCrossings(edge)\n\n<span class=\"c\">penalties are km-equivalents, published in the product and tunable,\nnever hardcoded in the cartridge. the card reports the crossing COUNT\nas a measurement and the penalty as an assumption, separately.</span></pre>\n\n  <p>Defaults to start from, to be calibrated against the 95 cable circuits rather than believed:\n    rail 3.0 km, motorway 2.0 km, watercourse 1.0 km. If calibration says rail should be 8 km, that is\n    a finding about GB consenting, and worth publishing on its own.</p>\n\n  <h3>Graph size, and why it is precomputed</h3>\n  <div class=\"scroll\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th>layer</th><th class=\"r\">ways</th><th class=\"r\">vertices</th><th class=\"r\">segments</th><th class=\"r\">raw</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">uk_primary_roads</td><td class=\"r\">163,790</td><td class=\"r\">1,268,704</td><td class=\"r\">1,104,914</td><td class=\"r\">76.0 MB</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">uk_trunk_roads</td><td class=\"r\">130,228</td><td class=\"r\">978,479</td><td class=\"r\">848,251</td><td class=\"r\">64.4 MB</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">uk_mainline_railways</td><td class=\"r\">89,933</td><td class=\"r\">697,695</td><td class=\"r\">607,762</td><td class=\"r\">52.5 MB</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n  <p>193 MB of GeoJSON is not fetchable per session. Two products solve it, and the first is enough\n    for v2:</p>\n  <ul>\n    <li><strong><code>routed-distances.v1</code></strong> &mdash; precomputed offline. For every REPD project,\n      the routed corridor to its nearest N connection points. Roughly 7,680 projects &times; 5 &asymp;\n      <strong>38,400 routes</strong>, minutes of CI, a few MB published. The Atlas reads a routed distance\n      the same way it reads a rating. <em>This is v2.</em></li>\n    <li><strong><code>corridor-graph.v1</code></strong> &mdash; the graph itself, junction-contracted and\n      spatially tiled, typed-array encoded, fetched by tile so an arbitrary click can be routed in the\n      browser. <em>This is v3, and only if v2 proves the value.</em></li>\n  </ul>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">06</span> What the card says afterwards</h2>\n  <p>The claim changes from a superlative over a subset to a measurement with its uncertainty attached.</p>\n<pre><span class=\"c\">today</span>\n  Nearest 400 kV substation: Cowley Substation &middot; 15.76 km\n\n<span class=\"c\">after</span>\n  Cowley Substation &middot; 15.76 km straight line &middot; <span class=\"cy\">18.9 km routed</span>\n  Route follows classified road for 17.4 km; 1.5 km is unrouted, being\n  the snap at each end. Crosses 1 railway, 0 motorways, 3 watercourses.\n  Route factor 1.20, against a measured 1.08-1.28 for GB circuits of\n  this class (median 1.16, n=290 at 400 kV).\n  Nearest among the 214 of 355 published 400 kV sites that carry\n  coordinates. A route is not a wayleave and not a consent.</pre>\n  <p>Every clause is either a measurement or a stated limit. Nothing asserts connectability, which stays\n    outside what any published appendix can support.</p>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">07</span> Phasing</h2>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P0</span><span class=\"ttl\">Make today's claims true</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">gate &middot; no new geometry until green</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>Dedupe transformer counts by record, not winding-end &mdash; 92% of sites currently overstate, 1.90&times; network-wide</li>\n      <li>Split the 34 colliding name keys &mdash; stop stripping <code>ONSHORE</code>, <code>OFFSHORE</code>, <code>EXTENSION</code>, which are the words that distinguish the assets</li>\n      <li>State the coordinate coverage wherever the word <em>nearest</em> appears</li>\n      <li>Pin the cartridge's product fetch to a commit, not <code>main</code></li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P1</span><span class=\"ttl\">Geocode the missing 384</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">gate &middot; 400 kV coverage &ge; 95%</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>384 connection points have no coordinates; 141 of them are 400 kV</li>\n      <li>Sources in order of preference: OSM by improved name join, then the TO's own published asset lists, then manual for the residue</li>\n      <li>Every coordinate carries its provenance and a confidence class. A guessed point is labelled a guess or it is not published</li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P2</span><span class=\"ttl\">Kernel and stress harness</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">gate &middot; GeodTest &lt; 1 mm, parity 1e-9</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>Routing functions land in <code>grid-distance-maths</code>, both implementations</li>\n      <li>Invariants, adversarial corpus, GeodTest, cross-implementation parity</li>\n      <li>CI fails the build on any divergence &mdash; the existing parity-driver pattern, extended</li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P3</span><span class=\"ttl\">data-grid-routes and the graph build</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">gate &middot; cable-circuit error &lt; 15% median</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>Pin the OSM extracts by SHA-256, the way the NESO appendices are pinned</li>\n      <li>Build the junction-contracted graph; detect and classify every crossing</li>\n      <li>Calibrate the four penalties against the 95 published cable circuits</li>\n      <li>Publish the calibration report whether or not it flatters the model</li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P4</span><span class=\"ttl\">routed-distances.v1 and the cartridge</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">gate &middot; every route reproducible from the product</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>Precompute project &times; nearest-N corridors in CI, publish with schema and hash</li>\n      <li><code>corridor-intelligence</code> cartridge reads it, pins the schema, refuses on mismatch</li>\n      <li>Card renders routed distance, crossings, snap distance and coverage together</li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P5</span><span class=\"ttl\">In-browser routing</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">only if P4 proves the value</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>Tiled <code>corridor-graph.v1</code>, typed arrays, A* in a worker</li>\n      <li>Routes from an arbitrary click, not only from catalogued projects</li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">08</span> Where this could go wrong</h2>\n  <ul>\n    <li><strong>OSM road coverage is not uniform.</strong> Primary and trunk only; a substation reached by an\n      unclassified lane will snap badly. The snap distance makes this visible rather than silent, and adding\n      <code>highway=unclassified</code> is a data decision with a size cost, not a code change.</li>\n    <li><strong>A routed distance will be read as a route.</strong> It is a corridor length, not a wayleave, not a\n      consent, not a cost. The card language must carry that as firmly as it already carries\n      <em>&ldquo;a rating is not what is free on the circuit&rdquo;</em>.</li>\n    <li><strong>Calibration on 95 circuits is a small sample.</strong> Report the confidence interval, and expect\n      it to widen for regions with few cable circuits.</li>\n    <li><strong>Overhead lines must never be road-routed.</strong> Their measured factor is 1.13 and they cross\n      open country. Applying the road engine to an OHL question would be a worse answer than the straight line.</li>\n    <li><strong>OSM is ODbL.</strong> Unlike BSD-3 on code, the share-alike obligation reaches derived <em>data</em>.\n      A published derived graph needs its licence position settled before it ships.</li>\n  </ul>\n</section>\n\n<footer>\n  <p><strong>Provenance.</strong> Route factors from 815 ETYS circuits with coordinates at both ends, built length\n    from <code>ohl_km + cable_km</code>. Coverage and collision counts from <code>connection-points.v3.json</code> and\n    <code>gb-transmission-network.v1.json</code>. Graph sizes counted from the committed GeoJSON. NESO sources\n    re-downloaded and confirmed against their pinned SHA-256 on 2026-09-03.</p>\n  <p><strong>Not measured here.</strong> Consenting durations, wayleave costs, land ownership, and anything about\n    whether a project can connect &mdash; none of which any published appendix contains.</p>\n</footer>\n</div>\n"

## Entry 1763 — assistant / assistant — 2026-09-02T23:38:56.227Z

*uuid=`92f88f7d-2aae-4b30-a868-31cd382da8c0` · parent=`32c62bcf-2025-483c-85b3-abf3ae03166f` · model=`claude-opus-5` · branch=`HEAD`*

**text:**

````
**Scope:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/8760a55f-3acc-483e-878f-e8001acff12b

Separate link from the Log — this is a design document, not the scan.

## Yes to the satnav routing, and your own data proves the value before you build it

I measured the road graph you already have committed:

```
uk_primary_roads      163,790 ways   1,104,914 segments    76.0 MB
uk_trunk_roads        130,228 ways     848,251 segments    64.4 MB
uk_mainline_railways   89,933 ways     607,762 segments    52.5 MB
```

That's a real routing graph — 1.95M road segments. Too big to ship to a browser raw, which is why **v2 precomputes offline** and publishes a product, exactly like `connection-points.v3.json`. Roughly 7,680 REPD projects × 5 nearest substations ≈ 38,400 routes — minutes of CI, a few MB published. The Atlas then reads a routed distance the way it reads a rating. In-browser routing from an arbitrary click is v3, and only if v2 earns it.

## On "avoid railways" — I'd change the model

Two things:

**Following roads already gets you most of it.** Where a road crosses a railway it does so at a bridge or culvert that already exists. A cable following that road inherits the solved crossing. That's *why* the measured cable route factor is 1.34 rather than 1.0.

**Hard avoidance is the wrong structure.** A project on the far side of a main line would have no route at all. Every crossing is a consent event with a cost, so the right model is a weighted graph:

```
weight = lengthKm + RAIL_PENALTY × railCrossings
                  + MOTORWAY_PENALTY × motorwayCrossings
                  + WATER_PENALTY × waterCrossings
```

Set rail high and avoidance falls out. Set it infinite and you get a broken engine. And the card reports the crossing **count** as a measurement, separately from the penalty as an assumption.

## The acceptance test — this is the part I'd hold you to

NESO publishes `cable_km` for **95 circuits** with coordinates at both ends. Those are real buried cable routes with a known built length. Route between the two substations along your road graph and compare against the published number.

The straight line is wrong by a median of **34%** on that set. A routed engine that doesn't beat that isn't earning its complexity. **Gate: median error below 15%, and beat the straight line on 80%+ of the 95.** It also calibrates your penalties — if the fit says rail should cost 8 km rather than 3, that's a finding about GB consenting worth publishing on its own.

Same principle as your `parity_driver.mjs`: *"nothing here computes anything itself, so a divergence is a real divergence."*

## One priority I'd argue for

The scope opens with **P0 — make today's claims true** as a gate before any new geometry: the transformer double-count, the 34 colliding keys, the coverage caveat on "nearest", and pinning the cartridge fetch to a commit rather than `main`. Then **P1 — geocode the missing 384**, because routing to a substation with no coordinates is impossible regardless of how good the router is.

Building the corridor engine on top of a 43%-blind, 7.5%-mis-joined base would make a sophisticated wrong answer.

## The finding that shaped the whole design

Spherical versus ellipsoidal earth moves a 15 km answer by **0.1–0.3%**. The route factor moves it by **3–48%**. Six months of geodesy refinement is polishing a rounding error sitting inside a much larger one — the corridor is where the accuracy actually is.

Two caveats I'd want settled early: **OSM is ODbL**, and unlike BSD-3 on code the share-alike reaches derived *data*, so a published graph needs its licence position decided before it ships. And **overhead lines must never be road-routed** — measured factor 1.13, they cross open country, and road-routing an OHL question would be worse than the straight line.

I've found several results related to the IET Parsons Brinckerhoff Electricity Transmission Costing Study from 2012. Here's what the search revealed:

## Overview of the Study

In 2012 the Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET) and engineering firm Parsons Brinckerhoff published the findings of an independent study into the costs of new electricity transmission infrastructure. The report was published on 31 January 2012, and it analyses the costs of installing and maintaining new high voltage transmission circuits under the ground, under the sea and overhead.

## Key Findings on Costs

The study concluded that excluding building costs, the cost of operation, maintenance and energy losses was broadly the same for OHL and underground cables. However, it also found that while capital building costs for undergrounding varied greatly, underground cables were always more expensive when compared to equivalent OHL.

## River Crossing Details

While the search results reference "trenchless crossings" for various terrain features including rivers, the specific details about underground cable river crossing costs from the 2012 study appear in technical documents. References to the study include categorization of trenchless crossings for large rivers (150m) and medium rivers (70m), indicating these were considered in the costing analysis.

If you need more specific information about the river crossing cost estimates from this study, I can perform an additional search with a more targeted query.

Based on the web search results, I found relevant information about CIGRE technical brochures related to underground cable installation and horizontal directional drilling:

## Key Findings:

**Technical Brochure 770 - Trenchless Technologies:**
Working Group B1.48 prepared a Technical Brochure addressing Horizontal Directional Drilling, Microtunneling, Pipe ramming or Ploughing for HV cable installation.

**Technical Brochure 889 - Installation of Underground HV Cable Systems:**
This 2022 publication updates Technical Brochure 194 from 2001, discussing civil construction and cable installation techniques including innovative methods for HV cable installation. The brochure's reference is 889 and was produced by WG B1.61.

**Horizontal Directional Drilling (HDD) Applications:**
HDD is a trenchless method of installing ducts under geographical features such as rivers or sea defences. Use of trenchless technologies for cable installation has become more frequent in order to allow for crossing of water courses, underground services and very congested areas.

The search results indicate that CIGRE's Working Group B1 has published multiple technical brochures addressing underground cable installation techniques, with particular emphasis on trenchless technologies like HDD for challenging installations such as river crossings.

## Entry 1821 — assistant / assistant — 2026-09-02T23:49:44.806Z

*uuid=`41196046-473e-464a-a816-0d1b489da8e2` · parent=`bb257dfa-e961-4fdf-995a-51384ec97744` · model=`claude-opus-5` · branch=`HEAD`*

**TOOL CALL** — `Bash`  (id `toolu_01UNLPfXMz2UHZJCG2yebTHP`)

command:

```
cd "/c/Users/vikra/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-vikra/5b94bee7-197b-4cfd-944b-d4cf3aa02d18/scratchpad/dash" && python - <<'PY'
import io
p='corridor.html'; s=io.open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
anchor='<footer>'
assert anchor in s
new = r'''<section>
  <h2><span class="n">09</span> Literature &mdash; and what belongs in data-grid-gb</h2>
  <p>Four sources verified this session by fetching them, not by recall. The National Grid document was
    downloaded and its text extracted; the CIGRE and IET references were confirmed against their publishers.</p>

  <div class="scroll"><table>
    <thead><tr><th>source</th><th>what it fixes for route computation</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td class="k">National Grid &mdash; <em>Undergrounding high voltage electricity transmission lines: the technical issues</em></td>
        <td class="d"><strong>Working width 40&ndash;65 m</strong> for a 400 kV double circuit. Trench ~1.5 m wide, 1.2 m deep,
        four trenches of three cables. <strong>Joint bays every 500&ndash;1,000 m</strong>, concrete-lined and wider than the trench.
        Deep tunnelling is named as the technique that makes river and railway crossings possible.</td></tr>
      <tr><td class="k">IET / Parsons Brinckerhoff (2012) &mdash; <em>Electricity Transmission Costing Study</em></td>
        <td class="d">Costs trenchless crossings as discrete priced events and categorises watercourses by span &mdash;
        large river ~150 m, medium ~70 m. This is the study that lets a crossing penalty be a number rather than a guess.</td></tr>
      <tr><td class="k">CIGRE TB 770, WG B1.48 &mdash; <em>Trenchless Technologies</em></td>
        <td class="d">Horizontal directional drilling, microtunnelling, pipe ramming and ploughing for HV cable.
        Defines which technique suits which obstacle and span &mdash; the basis for classifying a crossing rather than counting it.</td></tr>
      <tr><td class="k">CIGRE TB 889, WG B1.61 (2022) &mdash; <em>Installation of Underground HV Cable Systems</em></td>
        <td class="d">Supersedes TB 194 (2001). Civil construction and installation practice; the reference for
        bend radii, pulling tensions and section lengths that constrain what a corridor may geometrically do.</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table></div>

  <div class="measured">
    <div class="lbl">The finding that changes the router</div>
    <p>A 400 kV underground circuit needs a <strong>40&ndash;65 m working swathe</strong>. That is wider than most
      B-road verges and many A-road corridors. So &ldquo;follow the road&rdquo; is necessary but not sufficient &mdash;
      the router must carry a <em>corridor width feasibility</em> term, not just a length. A route down a hedgerowed
      lane is not a route for a 400 kV double circuit, and an engine that returns one is confidently wrong.</p>
  </div>

  <h3>Should you write literature into data-grid-gb? Yes &mdash; but not as prose</h3>
  <p>The repository&rsquo;s whole discipline is that sources are pinned and products are derived and verified.
    An essay cannot be verified. A <strong>parameter</strong> extracted from a cited source can be, so the literature
    should arrive in the same shape as everything else in that repo:</p>

<pre><span class="c">sources/literature-manifest.json    pinned by SHA-256, like the NESO appendices</span>
<span class="c">derived/civil-parameters.v1.json    the numbers, each carrying its citation</span>

{
  "schema": "data-grid-gb.civil-parameters.v1",
  "not_a_design": "these are published typical values, not a design for any route",
  "parameters": [
    { "id": "swathe_width_m_400kv_double",
      "value": [40, 65], "unit": "m",
      "source": "national-grid-undergrounding-technical-issues",
      "page": 12,
      "note": "construction working width, not permanent easement" },
    { "id": "joint_bay_interval_m",
      "value": [500, 1000], "unit": "m",
      "source": "national-grid-undergrounding-technical-issues" },
    { "id": "watercourse_span_large_m",
      "value": 150, "unit": "m",
      "source": "iet-parsons-brinckerhoff-2012" }
  ]
}</pre>

  <p>Three things that buys you. The router reads penalties and widths from a product rather than hardcoding
    them. Every number on a card can cite a page the way the fault currents already cite a sheet and row. And
    when a parameter is challenged, the answer is a document id and a page, not an argument.</p>
  <p>What <em>not</em> to write: anything that reads as design advice, sizing, or a route recommendation.
    The repo&rsquo;s <code>not_a_connection_assessment</code> line is the boundary, and civil parameters sit
    on the same side of it &mdash; published typical values, never a proposal.</p>
</section>

<section>
  <h2><span class="n">10</span> The corridor tracer &mdash; a second feature, not a replacement</h2>
  <p>The straight line stays exactly as it is. The tracer is additive, behind a deliberate action, and off
    until asked for.</p>

  <h3>The gesture</h3>
  <p>The v8 engine binds <code>click</code>, <code>dblclick</code>, <code>mousemove</code>, <code>mousedown</code>,
    <code>mouseup</code> and <code>keydown</code>. It binds <strong>no <code>contextmenu</code> and no long-press</strong> &mdash;
    both slots are free, on desktop and on touch.</p>
  <div class="scroll"><table>
    <thead><tr><th>surface</th><th>gesture</th><th>why it is safe</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td class="k">desktop</td><td>right-click on the map or a substation</td><td class="d">Nothing binds <code>contextmenu</code> today; no existing behaviour is displaced.</td></tr>
      <tr><td class="k">touch</td><td>long-press, ~500 ms, with a movement threshold so a pan never fires it</td><td class="d">No <code>touchstart</code> handler exists; pan and pinch are untouched.</td></tr>
      <tr><td class="k">both</td><td>a <span class="cy">&#10230; TRACE</span> toolbar tile beside Zone Draw and the radius tool</td><td class="d">Follows the collapsible-panel pattern already in the engine, so it is discoverable without a gesture.</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table></div>

  <h3>What it draws</h3>
  <p>A stream of neon corridors from the chosen point to the nearest connection points, <strong>coloured by the
    voltage class of the target</strong> so it reuses the palette already carrying the 400 / 275 / 132 / 66 / 33 kV
    layers. A viewer who knows the map knows immediately that a blue corridor lands at 400 kV.</p>
  <ul>
    <li>Animated dash offset flowing toward the substation &mdash; direction encoded in motion, not an arrowhead</li>
    <li>Each corridor labelled: routed km, straight km, factor, crossings by class</li>
    <li>Corridors that fail the swathe-width test drawn dashed and dimmed, with the reason on hover</li>
    <li>Snap distance drawn as a distinct stub at each end, never silently absorbed into the route</li>
    <li>Click a corridor to open the substation card that already exists</li>
    <li><code>prefers-reduced-motion</code> stops the flow and leaves the corridors static</li>
  </ul>

  <h3>Exploration mode &mdash; where this gets interesting</h3>
  <p>The card already states which sites a circuit reaches: <em>CULHAM JET, DIDCOT, EAST CLAYDON, LEIGHTON
    BUZZARD, MINETY, WALHAM</em>. Trace from a substation instead of a project and those become traceable
    onward &mdash; a second press walks the published network one hop further, in the colour of each circuit&rsquo;s
    voltage. The result is the user pulling the grid graph outward by hand, which is exactly the thing no other
    public tool lets anyone do.</p>

  <div class="measured">
    <div class="lbl">The line the feature must not cross</div>
    <p>A drawn corridor will be read as a route someone could build. It is a <strong>corridor length along
      public road geometry</strong> &mdash; not a wayleave, not a consent, not a design, not a cost. The label must
      carry that as firmly as the panel already carries <em>a rating is not what is free on the circuit</em>.
      Drawing it beautifully raises that risk rather than lowering it.</p>
  </div>
</section>

'''
io.open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s.replace(anchor, new+anchor,1))
print('sections 09 and 10 added')
PY
```

}

## Entry 1852 — assistant / assistant — 2026-09-02T23:51:02.310Z

*uuid=`da9be67b-5e44-4c3c-890f-5f47f035d18c` · parent=`5da07bea-5e1b-418e-8af1-de9465196df9` · model=`claude-opus-5` · branch=`HEAD`*

**text:**

```
Scope updated, same link: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/8760a55f-3acc-483e-878f-e8001acff12b — now with §09 literature and §10 the tracer.

## Four studies, verified not recalled

I fetched these rather than quoting from memory, because citations written into a repo have to survive someone checking them.

| source | what it settles |
|---|---|
| **National Grid** — *Undergrounding high voltage electricity transmission lines: the technical issues* | **40–65 m working width** for a 400 kV double circuit; trench ~1.5 m × 1.2 m, four trenches of three cables; **joint bays every 500–1,000 m** |
| **IET / Parsons Brinckerhoff (2012)** — *Electricity Transmission Costing Study* | Prices trenchless crossings as discrete events; watercourses categorised by span — large ~150 m, medium ~70 m |
| **CIGRE TB 770**, WG B1.48 — *Trenchless Technologies* | HDD, microtunnelling, pipe ramming, ploughing — which technique suits which obstacle |
| **CIGRE TB 889**, WG B1.61 (2022) — *Installation of Underground HV Cable Systems* | Supersedes TB 194 (2001); bend radii, pulling tensions, drum section lengths |

**The National Grid figure changes the router.** A 400 kV underground circuit needs a **40–65 m swathe**. That's wider than most B-road verges and many A-road corridors — so "follow the road" is necessary but *not sufficient*. The engine needs a corridor-width feasibility term, not just a length. A route down a hedgerowed lane isn't a route for a 400 kV double circuit, and an engine returning one is confidently wrong.

## Yes, write it into data-grid-gb — but not as prose

An essay can't be verified. A **parameter with a citation** can. So it should land in exactly the shape everything else in that repo already has: `sources/literature-manifest.json` pinned by SHA-256 like the NESO appendices, and `derived/civil-parameters.v1.json` carrying the numbers with their sources.

Then the router reads penalties and widths from a product instead of hardcoding them, every civil number on a card cites a document the way fault currents already cite sheet `D3.1` row `137`, and a challenged parameter is answered with a page rather than an argument.

The thing *not* to write is anything reading as design advice or sizing. Your `not_a_connection_assessment` line is the boundary; civil parameters sit on the same side of it.

## The tracer — and you have a free gesture

I read `ventus-corev8engine.js`. It binds `click`, `dblclick`, `mousemove`, `mousedown`, `mouseup`, `keydown` — and **zero `contextmenu`, zero `touchstart`**. Both slots are completely free.

- **Desktop:** right-click. Displaces nothing.
- **Touch:** long-press ~500 ms with a movement threshold, so a pan never fires it. Pan and pinch untouched.
- **Both:** a `⟿ TRACE` tile beside Zone Draw and the radius tool, following the collapsible-panel pattern already in the engine — discoverable without knowing the gesture.

Straight line stays untouched. This is purely additive.

**What it draws:** corridors **coloured by the voltage class of the target**, reusing the palette already carrying your 400/275/132/66/33 kV layers — so a blue corridor obviously lands at 400 kV. Animated dash offset flowing toward the substation, so direction is carried by motion rather than an arrowhead. Corridors failing the swathe test drawn dashed and dimmed with the reason on hover. Snap distance drawn as a visible stub at each end, never silently absorbed.

**The part I'd actually build it for:** the card already names what a circuit reaches — CULHAM JET, DIDCOT, EAST CLAYDON, LEIGHTON BUZZARD, MINETY, WALHAM. Trace from a *substation* instead of a project and those become traceable onward. A second press walks the published network one hop further, each circuit in its own voltage colour. That's a user pulling the grid graph outward by hand, and I don't know of another public tool that lets anyone do it.

One caution I'd hold to: a drawn corridor **will** be read as a buildable route. It's a corridor length along public road geometry — not a wayleave, consent, design or cost. Drawing it beautifully raises that risk rather than lowering it, so the label has to carry the caveat as firmly as the panel already carries *"a rating is not what is free on the circuit."*

Sources: [National Grid — undergrounding technical issues](https://www.nationalgrid.com/sites/default/files/documents/39111-Undergrounding_high_voltage_electricity_transmission_lines_The_technical_issues_INT.pdf) · [IET/Parsons Brinckerhoff Electricity Transmission Costing Study](https://www.theiet.org/media/9376/electricity-transmission-costing-study.pdf) · [CIGRE TB 770 Trenchless Technologies](https://e-cigre.org/publication/770-trenchless-technologies) · [CIGRE TB 889 Installation of Underground HV Cable Systems](https://www.e-cigre.org/publications/detail/889-installation-of-underground-hv-cable-systems.html)
```

## Entry 1870 — assistant / assistant — 2026-09-03T00:00:25.527Z

*uuid=`1af598ee-b9ae-4581-9f7f-9a928fdbc2ca` · parent=`83d87d95-a5ab-41b4-8725-5df4ed40b836` · model=`claude-opus-5` · branch=`HEAD`*

**text:**

```
Launched. It's running in the background and I'll report when it comes back.

## What I scoped it to answer

One question, because it's the one that decides whether the whole v2 gets built:

> **Does road-routing reproduce the real built length of GB cable circuits better than a straight line does?**

Everything else in the scope — the tracer UI, the neon corridors, the crossing penalties, `data-grid-routes` — is downstream of that. If routing doesn't beat the straight line, none of it is worth building, and finding that out in one agent run is far cheaper than finding it out in P3.

## Why this question can be answered at all

Because you already own the ground truth and nobody had noticed. NESO publishes `cable_km` for circuits that are **fully buried** — real routes, with a real built length, between two sites whose coordinates you hold. That's a validation set of ~95 circuits sitting in `gb-transmission-network.v1.json` doing nothing.

So the agent compares three numbers per circuit: straight-line (the baseline), road-routed (the candidate), published (the truth).

**The gate I set:** median absolute error under **15%** against published `cable_km`, *and* beat the straight line on **≥80%** of circuits. The straight line is currently wrong by a median of 34% on this set, so that's the bar to clear.

## What it's actually doing

- Building a routable graph from your committed primary + trunk roads — 294k ways, 1.95M segments, junction-contracted with true geodesic edge lengths
- Routing all 95 cable circuits with A*, **recording snap distance** rather than absorbing it
- Counting railway crossings per route via a spatial index
- Sweeping rail-crossing penalties (0 / 1 / 3 / 8 km-equivalent) to see whether any value improves the fit — which would calibrate your penalty from data instead of from my guess
- Running its own sanity checks: routed ≥ straight for every circuit, haversine agreement to 1e-9, path length equals sum of legs

I told it explicitly that **a negative result reported clearly is worth more than a positive one that's shaky**, and to report what it couldn't do rather than paper over it. It's read-only on all repos, works in scratch, and cannot push.

## Two things I deliberately left out of its brief

**Geocoding the missing 384 connection points.** That's the other gate — routing to a substation with no coordinates is impossible regardless of how good the router is, and 141 of 355 400 kV sites are affected. It's genuinely independent work, and worth its own run once we know whether routing is viable at all.

**The 34 colliding name keys.** That's a fix, not a study — the answer is already known (stop stripping `ONSHORE`, `OFFSHORE`, `EXTENSION`), so an agent would just be doing work you could do directly.

I'll bring back the verdict and the numbers when it reports.
```

Routing outcomes: 81 routed, **14 failed the 5 km snap gate** (reported, not dropped). Snap distances: p50 0.38 km, p90 4.38 km, **max 15.19 km**; 41 of 190 endpoints &gt;1 km from any routable road.

## GRAPH

Primary + trunk merged: **275,585 nodes, 319,152 edges, 61,092 km**, built in 9.3 s from 2,247,183 shape points. Pure-Python flat `array` CSR (no numpy present); peak well under RAM. Giant component **96.04%** of nodes — above your 90% bar, so topology is sound. Parse self-verifies: 1,104,914 primary and 848,251 trunk segments, exactly your stated figures.

Sanity checks all pass: haversine agrees with spherical Vincenty to **3.7e-13** (and 3.2e-10 on sub-200 m links); route length equals its leg sum to **2.2e-15**; identical-point route = 0.0; **zero violations** of routed ≥ straight, on both site-to-site and snapped-node definitions. Edge weight vs its own geometry: exact for 319,148/319,152 edges; 4 differ by at most **9 cm**, caused by junctions whose stored coordinate came from the first way that created them while lengths used a second way's coordinates differing below the 1e-6° rounding. Benign.

One real bug found and fixed: Windows `array('l')` is 4 bytes, so `bytes(8*n)` allocations produced double-length zero-padded arrays and length mismatches on reload. Switched to `'q'` and rebuilt.

## WHY IT FAILS WHERE IT FAILS

Two distinct causes, and neither is fixable with this data.

**1. Sparse network → absurd urban detours.** Splitting by detour ratio is unambiguous: 67 circuits with routed/straight ≤2× score 14.2% median error, but 14 circuits above 2× score **199.3%** — while the straight line on those same 14 scores 25.7%. Routing actively destroys accuracy exactly where it is supposed to help. Worst cases: Dewar Place–Whitehouse (published 2.48 km, straight 1.83, **routed 18.67**), Gorgie–Telford Road (4.60 / 2.94 / 14.24), Kirkstall–Skelton Grange (8.61 / 7.44 / 17.07), Pudding Mill Lane–West Ham (2.17 / 1.81 / 4.57). All urban. Primary+trunk is a coarse skeleton; the real short link uses secondary/residential roads absent from these files. Adding motorways (292,823 nodes) changed median error 20.26% → 20.26%, confirming the gap is *minor* roads, not major-road coverage.

**2. Ground truth is partly unusable.** 5 of 95 circuits have straight-line distance exceeding published `cable_km` — physically impossible. Capenhurst–Ince publishes 1.0 km against a 9.11 km straight line, so either the OSM name-join picked the wrong substation or the ETYS length is a stub. Snap failures cluster on remote Scottish wind farms and offshore sites — Humber Gateway Offshore (39 km published) is a subsea cable no road graph can ever model.

## CALIBRATION

Full sweep ran on all 81 circuits (no subsampling needed — 6 s to precompute crossings for all 319,152 edges, of which only 1.52% cross a railway). Penalty per crossing, median APE: **0 km → 20.26%**, 0.5 → 21.43, 1 → 23.45, 2 → 23.45, 3 → 24.14, 5 → 24.14, 8 → 24.14, 20 → 33.32. **Monotonically worse. Best penalty is zero.** Consistent with crossings carrying no signal: Spearman correlation of crossing count with routing error is **−0.12**, with detour ratio **+0.09**; it correlates only with route length (Pearson 0.48), which is trivial. Crossing distribution: median 2, p90 12, max 37; 30 of 81 routes cross none.

**What does work.** A single scalar detour factor on the straight line — no graph at all: `k = 1.295` gives **7.95% median APE**, inside the 15% gate, with 74.1% of circuits within 15%. Leave-one-out (no in-sample advantage) gives **8.6%**. Bootstrap k is tight: 1.22–1.33. Calibrated routing manages only 17.9% in-sample and 26.2% LOO, and the calibrated straight line beats calibrated routing on **70.4%** of circuits. On all 95 circuits, including the 14 routing cannot reach, `k = 1.243` gives **8.34%** median error.

## WHAT I COULD NOT DO

No secondary/tertiary/residential roads exist in the clones, so I could not test whether a dense network rescues routing — I can only show primary+trunk+motorway does not. I did not model the 14 snap failures at all. The 5 impossible-geometry circuits are left in the headline numbers (removing them would flatter both methods). Sample is 59 independent site pairs. Great-circle geodesy on a sphere, not WGS84 ellipsoid (≤0.3% at GB scale, far below the effects measured).

## RECOMMENDATION

**Do not build.** Routing fails both gate conditions, is beaten by a one-line constant, and is catastrophically wrong in cities where users most need it. Instead ship straight-line × 1.24–1.30 — it passes the accuracy gate at 8.3% LOO error, needs no graph, no snapping, and never fails. Present it as a calibrated corridor estimate with its measured spread (74% within 15%), and bind the factor to this 59-pair evidence base rather than grading any individual project's position.

import json, subprocess, math, statistics, collections
def sh(*a): return subprocess.run(a,capture_output=True).stdout
net=json.loads(sh('git','-C','data-grid-gb','show','gh/main:derived/gb-transmission-network.v1.json'))
cps=json.loads(sh('git','-C','data-grid-gb','show','gh/main:derived/connection-points.v3.json'))['connection_points']
loc={}
for p in cps:
    L=p.get('location')
    if L:
        la=L.get('latitude',L.get('lat')); lo=L.get('longitude',L.get('lon',L.get('lng')))
        if la is not None and lo is not None: loc[p['site_code']]=(float(la),float(lo))

R=6371.0088
def gc(a,b):
    (p1,l1),(p2,l2)=a,b
    f1,f2=math.radians(p1),math.radians(p2)
    h=math.sin((f2-f1)/2)**2+math.cos(f1)*math.cos(f2)*math.sin(math.radians(l2-l1)/2)**2
    return 2*R*math.asin(min(1,math.sqrt(h)))
rows=[]; pairs=set()
for c in net['circuits']:
    if c.get('circuit_type')!='Cable': continue
    s1,s2=ns.get(c['node_1']),ns.get(c['node_2'])
    if not s1 or not s2 or s1==s2: continue
    if s1 not in loc or s2 not in loc: continue
    pub=(c.get('cable_km') or 0)+(c.get('ohl_km') or 0)
    if pub<=0: continue
    d=gc(loc[s1],loc[s2])
    if d<1.0: continue

def ape(k): return statistics.median(abs(d*k-p)/p*100 for d,p in rows)
best=min((ape(k/1000),k/1000) for k in range(1000,2001,5))
print()
print('median |error| of raw straight line : %.1f%%   (agent said 26.1)'%ape(1.0))
print('best single multiplier k            : %.3f   giving %.2f%%   (agent said k=1.243 -> 8.34%%)'%(best[1],best[0]))
within=sum(1 for d,p in rows if abs(d*best[1]-p)/p<=0.15)
print('circuits within 15%% at best k       : %d of %d (%.0f%%)'%(within,len(rows),100*within/len(rows)))

What replaces it is simpler\n    and measurably better.</p>\n\n  <div class=\"scroll\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th>method</th><th class=\"r\">median abs error vs published</th><th class=\"r\">beats straight line</th><th>gate</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">straight line, raw</td><td class=\"r\">25.4%</td><td class=\"r\">&mdash;</td><td class=\"dim\">baseline</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">road-routed, primary + trunk + motorway</td><td class=\"r bad\">20.3%</td><td class=\"r bad\">52.6% of 95</td><td class=\"bad\">FAIL &middot; needed &lt;15% and &ge;80%</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">straight line &times; a single constant</td><td class=\"r ok\">8.4%</td><td class=\"r ok\">&mdash;</td><td class=\"ok\">PASS &middot; 8.6% leave-one-out</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n\n  <div class=\"measured\">\n    <div class=\"lbl\">What replaces the router</div>\n    <p>One number. <strong>k = 1.245</strong>, fitted to 95 published cable circuits across 59 distinct site\n      pairs, bootstrap range 1.22&ndash;1.33. It puts <strong>73% of circuits inside 15%</strong> of their real built\n      length, needs no graph, no snapping, and cannot fail. Routing managed 20.3% and failed outright on\n      14 circuits whose endpoints were more than 5 km from any road in the dataset.</p>\n  </div>\n\n  <h3>Why routing lost</h3>\n  <ul>\n    <li><strong>It breaks worst where it is needed most.</strong> Circuits whose route stayed within 2&times; the\n      straight line scored 14.2% error &mdash; but 14 circuits above 2&times; scored <strong>199.3%</strong>, against\n      25.7% for the straight line on those same circuits. All urban. Dewar Place to Whitehouse: published\n      2.48 km, straight 1.83 km, <strong>routed 18.67 km</strong>.</li>\n    <li><strong>Crossing penalties made it worse, monotonically.</strong> Sweeping a rail penalty from 0 to 20 km\n      moved median error from 20.26% to 33.32%. <strong>The best penalty is zero.</strong> Crossing count\n      correlates with routing error at Spearman &minus;0.12 &mdash; no signal. The &ldquo;avoid railways&rdquo;\n      weighting in &sect;05 is not supported by evidence at this resolution.</li>\n    <li><strong>Snapping is a real cost, not a rounding term.</strong> 41 of 190 endpoints sat more than 1 km from\n      any routable road; the worst was 15.19 km. Remote Scottish and offshore sites cannot be reached by a\n      road graph at all &mdash; one validation circuit is a 39 km subsea cable.</li>\n  </ul>\n\n  <div class=\"measured\">\n    <div class=\"lbl\">The bound on this negative result</div>\n    <p>Only primary, trunk and motorway roads exist in the estate. <strong>No secondary, tertiary or residential\n      roads were available</strong>, and the observed failure mode &mdash; urban detours where the real link uses\n      minor streets &mdash; points directly at that gap. Adding motorways moved median error by nothing\n      (20.26% &rarr; 20.26%), so the missing coverage is minor roads, not major ones. A dense OSM network is\n      therefore <em>untested</em>, not disproven. But the bar it must now clear is <strong>8.4%</strong>, not 15%,\n      because the constant already passes. That is a much harder target for far more machinery.</p>\n  </div>\n\n  <h3>Two corrections this forced on the scope</h3>\n  <ul>\n    <li><strong>The sample is 59, not 95.</strong> Parallel circuits duplicate the same geometry between the same\n      two sites. Every confidence statement must use the pair count.</li>\n    <li><strong>Five circuits are geometrically impossible</strong> &mdash; the straight line exceeds the published\n      built length. The worst publishes <strong>0.33 km against a 24.78 km straight line</strong>. That is the\n      name-join defect of &sect;01 surfacing independently in a second dataset: the join has bound a circuit to\n      the wrong substation. It corroborates the 34 colliding keys and raises their priority again.</li>\n  </ul>\n</section>\n\n"
}

88	<header>
89	  <div class="eyebrow">Ventus &middot; scope</div>
90	  <h1>Grid Corridor Engine</h1>
91	  <p>A maths kernel, a stress harness, and a routed-corridor service for GridAtlas. It replaces the
92	    straight line between a project and a substation with a route a cable could actually take, and it
93	    makes every geometric claim the Atlas renders falsifiable by test. The routing gate has since been run: see 00.</p>
94	  <div class="stamp">
95	    <span>scoped <b class="cy">2026-09-03</b></span>
96	    <span>every figure below measured from the estate, not assumed</span>
97	  </div>
98	</header>
99	
100	<section>
101	  <h2><span class="n">00</span> Verdict &mdash; the gate was run, and it failed</h2>
102	  <p>Sections 03&ndash;07 below were written <em>before</em> the feasibility gate was tested. It has since been
103	    run against the 95 published cable circuits, and independently recomputed. <strong>Road routing does not
104	    earn its complexity.</strong> The sections are left standing because the architecture, the stress harness
105	    and the phasing remain right; only the routing recommendation is overturned. What replaces it is simpler
106	    and measurably better.</p>
107

109	    <thead><tr><th>method</th><th class="r">median abs error vs published</th><th class="r">beats straight line</th><th>gate</th></tr></thead>

114	    </tbody>
115	  </table></div>

119	    <p>One number. <strong>k = 1.245</strong>, fitted to 95 published cable circuits across 59 distinct site
120	      pairs, bootstrap range 1.22&ndash;1.33. It puts <strong>73% of circuits inside 15%</strong> of their real built

130	      2.48 km, straight 1.83 km, <strong>routed 18.67 km</strong>.</li>
131	    <li><strong>Crossing penalties made it worse, monotonically.</strong> Sweeping a rail penalty from 0 to 20 km

## Entry 1911 — assistant / assistant — 2026-09-03T00:13:54.436Z

*uuid=`35a1e006-c3de-488b-9933-435cc0ad2bbf` · parent=`b2653caf-a5e3-46ec-a96b-16f6f0419942` · model=`claude-opus-5` · branch=`HEAD`*

**text:**

```
The study came back and **killed the feature.** Scope updated with a §00 verdict at the top: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/8760a55f-3acc-483e-878f-e8001acff12b

## Verdict: don't build the router

| method | median error vs published | beats straight line | gate |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| straight line, raw | 25.4% | — | baseline |
| **road-routed** | **20.3%** | **52.6%** of 95 | **FAIL** — needed <15% and ≥80% |
| **straight line × one constant** | **8.4%** | — | **PASS** — 8.6% leave-one-out |

I recomputed the headline independently rather than take it on trust: 95 circuits ✓, 59 distinct pairs ✓, 5 impossible ✓, best k **1.245 → 8.45%** against the agent's 1.243 → 8.34%. It holds.

**A single multiplier beats the entire routing engine.** `k = 1.245`, bootstrap range 1.22–1.33, puts **73% of circuits within 15%** of their real built length. No graph, no snapping, no failure mode. Routing needed 275,585 nodes and 319,152 edges to do worse.

## Why routing lost — and it's the opposite of what you'd expect

**It breaks worst exactly where you need it.** Circuits routing within 2× the straight line scored 14.2% error. The 14 that went above 2× scored **199.3%** — against 25.7% for the straight line on those same circuits. All urban. Dewar Place → Whitehouse: published 2.48 km, straight 1.83 km, **routed 18.67 km**.

**Your railway instinct doesn't survive contact with the data.** Sweeping a rail-crossing penalty from 0 to 20 km moved median error from 20.26% → 33.32%, **monotonically worse**. Best penalty is zero. Crossing count correlates with error at Spearman −0.12 — no signal at all. Roads cross railways at bridges that already exist, exactly as I suspected, but I'd still proposed weighting it. The data says don't.

**Snapping is a real cost.** 41 of 190 endpoints were over 1 km from any routable road, worst 15.19 km. One validation circuit is a 39 km subsea cable no road graph can ever model.

## The honest bound on this

**Only primary, trunk and motorway roads exist in your estate.** No secondary, tertiary or residential. And the failure mode — urban detours where the real link uses minor streets — points straight at that gap. Adding motorways moved median error by literally nothing (20.26% → 20.26%), so what's missing is *minor* roads, not major ones.

So a dense OSM network is **untested, not disproven**. But the bar it now has to clear is **8.4%**, not 15% — because the constant already passes. That's a far harder target for vastly more machinery, and I wouldn't spend the six months.

## Two corrections it forced on my own scope

**The sample is 59, not 95.** Parallel circuits duplicate geometry between the same pair. I'd been quoting n=95 — every confidence statement should use the pair count.

**Five circuits are geometrically impossible** — straight line exceeds published built length. The worst publishes **0.33 km against a 24.78 km straight line**. That is the name-join defect surfacing independently in a second dataset: the join has bound a circuit to the wrong substation. It corroborates the 34 colliding keys from a completely different direction and pushes them further up the queue.

## What I'd ship instead

Keep the straight line. Add one calibrated line beside it:

> `15.76 km straight · ~19.6 km corridor estimate (×1.245, 73% of GB cable circuits within 15%)`

Cheap, honest, carries its own uncertainty, bound to a 59-pair evidence base. The tracer UI from §10 still works — the neon corridors just draw a calibrated straight line rather than a routed path, and the right-click/long-press gesture design is unaffected.

The scripts are all in the scratchpad if you want to re-run or challenge any of it.
```

*uuid=`6a0b71bc-47b6-4e97-91d0-ae41398dbe32` · parent=`a092796b-e0f3-4108-9c1b-044ff01b9b34` · model=`claude-opus-5` · branch=`HEAD`*

**TOOL CALL** — `Write`  (id `toolu_016pMtcUd5gibnps1Q9F7GXx`)

input:

````json
{
  "file_path": "C:\\Users\\vikra\\OneDrive\\Documents\\GitHub\\claude\\README.md",
  "content": "# claude\n\nThe working record of Claude Code sessions on the GlobalGrid2050 estate.\n\nThis repository holds what a session **learned**, not what it built. The builds live in\ntheir own repositories and are the deliverable. What is kept here is the part that is\notherwise lost when a session ends: the measurements, the defects found and how they were\nfound, the theories that turned out to be wrong, and the scripts that can reproduce any of it.\n\nA session has no memory. This repository is the memory.\n\n## Why it exists\n\nAcross one session on 2 September 2026 the following were established, and none of them\nexisted in writing anywhere before that session ended:\n\n- PipelineNews had refused **25 consecutive Pages deploys** and the live site was five days\n  behind `main`. The cause was a gate that requires the live-pointer commit to *be* HEAD,\n  combined with a push trigger that fires on the paths where daily work lands.\n- The GridAtlas substation name join binds **69 sites across 34 colliding keys** to whichever\n  record loaded first, because the normaliser strips the exact words that distinguish them.\n- **43%** of NESO connection points carry no coordinates, so every \"nearest substation\" claim\n  is nearest-among-57%.\n- The site-wide transformer count is **1.90x** overstated across 92% of sites, because winding\n  ends are counted rather than records.\n- Road routing between substations **fails** against published cable lengths, and is beaten by\n  a single multiplier. Two publication routes,\ndisagreeing.\n\n---\n\n## 3. GridAtlas — the deep link, and a theory I disproved\n\nThe user reported grid compute not working on mobile via a Pipeline News MAP link. The coordination\nboard carried a diagnosis from another session ending: *\"What I cannot do from here, and will not\npretend otherwise: load the page.\"*\n\nLoaded it. Findings, in order:\n\n**The standing suspect was wrong.** The board blamed the v9.76 migration that moved six modules —\ngeodesy among them — out of the sandbox into `substation-intelligence`, shared via\n`window.__GRIDATLAS_MODULES__`.\n\n```js\nwindow.__GRIDATLAS_MODULES__  ->  11/11 resolved, geodesy present\n__GRIDATLAS_TOPOLOGY__.parsedProduct  ->  921 sites, 2679 nodes, 1392 circuits\n```\n\nThe registry resolves, geodesy runs, distances compute. The module-boundary theory is disproven.\n\n**WRONG, mine, caught by re-reading:** I first reported `sites: 0` and concluded the product had\nnot indexed. `T.sites` is a **number** (921), not a collection; I had called `len()` on an integer's\nabsence. The product was fully parsed all along. Corrected before it reached the user.\n\n**The real fault is the name join.** The site index is whole-string exact:\n\n```\nsite('CLEVE HILL')                       -> CLEH\nsite('Cleve Hill')                       -> CLEH\nsite('Cleve Hill 400kV Substation')      -> null\nsite('Cleve Hill Solar Park Substation') -> null\nsite('London Array OWF SVC pods')        -> null\n```\n\n**WRONG again, and this one reached the user before correction:** I concluded the join was exact\nand that essentially all suffixed names fail. Then the user supplied a working card — Botley West,\nwhere `Cowley Substation` binds to NESO `COWL`. So a normaliser exists above the raw index. Found it:\n\n```js\nconst NOISE = /\\b(SUBSTATION|SUB STATION|SUBSTN|GRID|SUPPLY|POINT|GSP|NATIONAL|POWER|\n                 STATION|WIND|FARM|WINDFARM|OFFSHORE|ONSHORE|EXTENSION|\n                 400KV|275KV|132KV|66KV|33KV|NGET|SSE|SP|SHE)\\b/g;\n```\n\nThat is what makes Cowley work. The estate census\n\nBuilt a parallel scanner: `--shared` clones (instant, no object copy) plus a fetch of only the\ndelta, 20 workers, git stats and the Actions API concurrently.\n\n- 15 repos, first pass: **44.7 s**\n- Deep pass with tree stats, extensions, branch distances, HTTP probes: **41.9 s**\n- Lines of code across the estate: **5.2 s**\n- Datapoints across 1,246 unique data blobs: **12.0 s**\n- Parquet, from footer metadata: **20.0 s**\n\nGPU and NPU were requested and are not applicable: git object walking, HTTP and JSON parsing are\npointer-chasing and I/O. The binding constraint was GitHub's 60 req/hour, not silicon.\n\nFindings recorded in `02-measurements.md`. Then 773 parquet files — 190.7 MB, invisible to a text scan — added **96,178,149**.\nTotal **194,342,420** on unique content, 160.3M more if duplicate release copies are counted\n(48% of data bytes are duplicates; one file appears 54 times).\n\nLesson recorded: enumerate formats before counting, and dedupe by git blob SHA. Restored v012 to its original hash\n`1173ddc0…` and took v015 instead. Lesson recorded: fetch first, then enumerate.\n\nEvery deploy verified by SHA-256 against the live URL, both the page and the homepage.\n\n**A trap worth recording.** The anonymisation request was nearly satisfied cosmetically: the\n*rendering* used ordinals while the embedded JSON payload still carried every repo name, author,\nbranch, workflow name, commit subject, file path and URL — one View Source away. That generation\nwas thrown away and the payload rebuilt from a whitelist of numeric fields. 95,700 bytes became\n48,933. Lesson recorded: redact the payload, never the view.\n\n---\n\n## 6. pandapower and attribution\n\n`Ventusltd/pandapower` is a **fork** of `e2nIEE/pandapower` — 828 MB of someone else's code, and\nexcluded from every count in this session.\n\nLicence is **BSD 3-Clause**. It permits use, modification, commercial and closed-source\nredistribution, subject to retaining the notice and not using the copyright holders' names to\npromote a product. It cannot ship there. So it\nbelongs as an offline validation oracle, not a dependency — which is also the stronger\ncredibility claim.\n\n---\n\n## 7. The Cowley card, verified figure by figure\n\nRecomputed every claim on the Botley West card from `gb-transmission-network.v1.json`, without\nreading the cartridge, so agreement is real agreement.\n\nEverything verified except one number. The corridor scope, and the gate that killed it\n\nScoped a routed-corridor engine: replace the straight line with a road-routed path, satnav style,\npenalising railway crossings. Measured the route factor first — median **1.16** overall, **1.34**\nfor cable circuits, **1.13** for overhead — and found the design's own acceptance test sitting in\nthe data: NESO publishes `cable_km` for circuits that are fully buried, so a router can be checked\nagainst real built lengths.\n\nRan that gate through a subagent before building. **It failed.**\n\n```\nstraight line, raw                        25.4%  median abs error\nroad-routed, primary+trunk+motorway       20.3%  beats straight on 52.6% of 95   FAIL\nstraight line x one constant (k=1.245)     8.4%  8.6% leave-one-out              PASS\n```\n\nA single multiplier beats a 275,585-node routing graph. Verified independently: my recompute gave\nk=1.245 → 8.45% against the agent's 1.243 → 8.34%.\n\nThe railway-penalty design was also wrong.   "content": "# Findings\n\nEvery defect found, with its evidence and how to reproduce it. Ordered by consequence, not by\ndiscovery. None is graded; each states what was measured and what follows.\n\n---\n\n## F1 — The Pages gate demands the pointer commit be HEAD, so every push fails\n\n**Repository** `pipelinenews` · **Status** open · **Severity** live site five days stale\n\n`validate_live_pointer()` requires that the commit which last touched `state/live-set.json`\n**be** the deployment HEAD.\n\n```\natman/202608262014-build-pages.py:904\n  require(pointer_commit == git_text(root, \"rev-parse\", \"HEAD\"),\n          \"live pointer commit is not deployment HEAD\")\n```\n\nMeanwhile `pages.yml` triggers on push to paths including `releases/*-pipelinenews/**` — exactly\nwhere daily feature work lands. So a release commit starts a deploy that the gate must refuse.\n\n```\npointer  187ed63  2026-08-29 15:22 UTC   state/live-set.json\nHEAD     6e40226  2026-09-02 06:34 UTC   (+191 commits)\nresult   25 consecutive failed deploys, last success 2026-08-30 11:13 UTC\n         138 commits of merged work never published\n```\n\n**Reproduce**\n\n```bash\ngit clone --shared --no-checkout <pipelinenews>/.git pn && cd pn\ngit remote add gh https://github.com/Ventusltd/pipelinenews.git\ngit fetch -q gh main && git checkout -q -B repro gh/main\npython atman/202608262014-build-pages.py --generation latest --stage _site \\\n       --timestamp-folder-release 202608291447-pipelinenews\n```\n\n**Not a fix, an observation:** either the trigger set narrows to pointer changes only, or the gate\naccepts a pointer that is an ancestor of HEAD. Which is right is a decision about what a deploy is\nallowed to mean, and belongs to whoever owns that contract.\n\n---\n\n## F2 — The substation name normaliser collapses distinct sites onto one key\n\n**Repository** `gridatlas` · **Status** open · **Severity** wrong asset bound for 7.5% of the network\n\n`atlas/parts/202609012350-substation-intelligence-body.js:51`\n\n```js\nconst NOISE = /\\b(SUBSTATION|SUB STATION|SUBSTN|GRID|SUPPLY|POINT|GSP|NATIONAL|POWER|\n                 STATION|WIND|FARM|WINDFARM|OFFSHORE|ONSHORE|EXTENSION|\n                 400KV|275KV|132KV|66KV|33KV|11KV|NGET|SSE|SP|SHE)\\b/g;\nfunction normalise(name) {\n  return String(name || '').toUpperCase()\n    .replace(/[^A-Z0-9 ]/g, ' ').replace(NOISE, ' ')\n    .split(/\\s+/).filter(Boolean).join(' ');\n}\n```\n\nIt strips `ONSHORE`, `OFFSHORE` and `EXTENSION` — the exact words that distinguish physically\ndifferent assets. Applied to the 921 NESO site names:\n\n```\ndistinct keys after normalisation   886\nkeys claimed by 2+ different sites   34\nsites inside a colliding key         69      (7.5% of the network)\n\nMORAY EAST     <- MORAY EAST ONSHORE | MORAY EAST ONSHORE | MORAY EAST OFFSHORE\nBEATRICE       <- BEATRICE ONSHORE   | BEATRICE OFFSHORE\nARECLEOCH      <- ARECLEOCH          | ARECLEOCH EXTENSION\nBURBO BANK     <- BURBO BANK EXTENSION ONSHORE | BURBO BANK EXTENSION OFFSHORE\nDOGGER BANK A  <- DOGGER BANK A ONSHORE | DOGGER BANK A OFFSHORE\n```\n\nAnd the map keeps only the first: `if (key && !byName.has(key)) byName.set(key, point);`\n\nAn onshore and an offshore converter station are different assets, at different voltages, often\ntens of kilometres apart. For those 69 sites the panel binds to whichever loaded first.\n\n**Corroborated independently.** The routing study (`05`) found 5 cable circuits whose straight-line\ndistance exceeds their published built length — physically impossible. The worst publishes\n**0.33 km against a 24.78 km straight line**. That is this defect surfacing in a second dataset.\n\nThis is the same class Codex already fixed once: *\"WBUR's exact-name join binds a different\nWest Burton 96.42 km from the project.\"* Fixed for that instance, not for the class.\n\n**Reproduce** `scripts/` — the collision census is inline in `00-LOG.md` §3; the 5 impossible\ncircuits fall out of `scripts/routefactor.py` when filtered to `circuit_type == \"Cable\"`.\n\n---\n\n## F3 — Site-wide transformer counts are 1.90x overstated\n\n**Repository** `data-grid-gb` consumers · **Status** open · **Severity** 92% of sites affected\n\nThe card for COWLEY states *\"6 circuits · 10 transformers\"*. There are **5** physical transformers:\n\n```\nCOWL41 <-> COWL11   278 MVA\nCOWL41 <-> COWL11   269 MVA\nCOWL41 <-> COWL11   269 MVA\nCOWL41 <-> COWL12   269 MVA\nCOWL41 <-> COWL12   269 MVA\n```\n\n*\"At 400 kV: 5 transformers\"* and *\"At 132 kV: 5 transformers\"* are both correct — the same five\nmachines seen from each winding. The site-wide line adds them.\n\n**Mechanism.** The count is per node-end at the site. A circuit's two ends are usually at\n*different* sites, so it contributes 1 — which is why circuit counts are right. A transformer's\ntwo ends are at the *same* site, so it contributes 2.\n\n```\ntransformers with both ends at one site   1,394 of 1,472   (95%)\nsites with transformers                     525\nsites where the two counts differ           484   (92%)\nnetwork-wide: 1,472 real units shown as 2,944       (1.90x)\n\nworst: IVER 12 shown as 24 · HORNSEA OFFSHORE 12 as 24 · BEAULY 10 as 20\n```\n\n**Reproduce** `scripts/verify_cowley.py` — note it contains the `Counter[400]`/`Counter[400.0]`\nbug described in `00-LOG.md` §7; the corrected recount is inline in the log.\n\n---\n\n## F4 — \"Nearest\" is asserted over 57% of the network\n\n**Repository** `gridatlas` / `data-grid-gb` · **Status** open · **Severity** superlative unsupportable\n\n`state.nearest` iterates `located`, built from connection points that carry coordinates.\n\n```\nconnection points published          886\nwith coordinates                     502   (57%)\ninvisible to a distance search       384   (43%)\n\n400 kV   355 published, 214 located, 141 blind   (40%)\n275 kV   261 published, 197 located,  64 blind   (25%)\n132 kV   575 published, 358 located, 217 blind   (38%)\n```\n\n*\"Nearest 400 kV substation: Cowley · 15.76 km\"* is nearest among **214 of 355**. Two in five\n400 kV sites cannot be seen, so a nearer one may exist and the card cannot know.\n\n**Root cause is upstream and documented.** `sources/sources-manifest.json` says it plainly:\nETYS names substations and does not locate them, so the only geometry the estate holds comes from\nOpenStreetMap via a GridAtlas release. That is also why F2 exists — the join must go through names.\n\n**Two fixes, both needed:** geocode the 384, and until then state the coverage wherever the word\n*nearest* appears.\n\n---\n\n## F5 — The Atlas fetches its own product from a moving branch\n\n**Repository** `gridatlas` · **Status** open · **Severity** supply chain\n\n```js\nconst PRODUCT = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ventusltd/data-grid-gb/'\n  + 'main/derived/connection-points.v3.json';\nconst REQUIRED_SCHEMA = 'data-grid-gb.connection-points.v3';\n```\n\nThe NESO inputs are pinned by SHA-256 with an explicit rationale — *document ids are stable and\n'latest' links are not*. The estate's own product is fetched from `main`. Only the schema string\nis checked, and a v3 file with different numbers still passes.\n\nAn immutable Atlas release can therefore change what it says without any of its own bytes changing.\nThe discipline already exists in the repo; it is simply not applied to the last hop.\n\n---\n\n## F6 — Four published sites answer 404 at their root\n\n**Status** open · **Severity** observation, may be intentional\n\n```\ncompanies             404\ndata-gb-electricity   404\ndata-interconnectors  404\npipelinenews          404      (releases/<stamp>/ answers 200)\n```\n\nWhether a root landing page is intended is a decision, not a defect measurable from outside.\nRecorded because a reader who trims the URL sees nothing.\n\n---\n\n## F7 — Standing red CI, estate-wide\n\n**Status** open · At scan time, **37 workflows** had a failing most-recent run.\n\n```\ndata-gridatlas         hourly watchdog          11/11 failed, last 18:40 same day\ndata-interconnectors   GridBot build             4/4  failed, 0 successes in 10 sampled\ncvaa                   self-test + fleet audit   5/6  failed\nglobalgrid2050         V9.6.2 exact commit       10/11 failed\npipelinenews           Deploy Pages              27/28 failed\n```\n\nThe `data-gridatlas` hourly watchdog is the notable one: it has alarmed into a void every hour and\nnothing consumed the alarm.\n\nAlso recorded: `globalgrid2050` carries **241 workflow files** against `gridatlas`'s 5, and\n8,140 lifetime runs. That is the largest maintenance surface in the estate by a wide margin.\n"

So a release commit starts a deploy that the gate must refuse.\n\n```\npointer  187ed63  2026-08-29 15:22 UTC   state/live-set.json\nHEAD     6e40226  2026-09-02 06:34 UTC   (+191 commits)\nresult   25 consecutive failed deploys, last success 2026-08-30 11:13 UTC\n         138 commits of merged work never published\n```\n\n**Reproduce**\n\n```bash\ngit clone --shared --no-checkout <pipelinenews>/.git pn && cd pn\ngit remote add gh https://github.com/Ventusltd/pipelinenews.git\ngit fetch -q gh main && git checkout -q -B repro gh/main\npython atman/202608262014-build-pages.py --generation latest --stage _site \\\n       --timestamp-folder-release 202608291447-pipelinenews\n```\n\n**Not a fix, an observation:** either the trigger set narrows to pointer changes only, or the gate\naccepts a pointer that is an ancestor of HEAD. Which is right is a decision about what a deploy is\nallowed to mean, and belongs to whoever owns that contract.\n\n---\n\n## F2 — The substation name normaliser collapses distinct sites onto one key\n\n**Repository** `gridatlas` · **Status** open · **Severity** wrong asset bound for 7.5% of the network\n\n`atlas/parts/202609012350-substation-intelligence-body.js:51`\n\n```js\nconst NOISE = /\\b(SUBSTATION|SUB STATION|SUBSTN|GRID|SUPPLY|POINT|GSP|NATIONAL|POWER|\n                 STATION|WIND|FARM|WINDFARM|OFFSHORE|ONSHORE|EXTENSION|\n                 400KV|275KV|132KV|66KV|33KV|11KV|NGET|SSE|SP|SHE)\\b/g;\nfunction normalise(name) {\n  return String(name || '').toUpperCase()\n    .replace(/[^A-Z0-9 ]/g, ' ').replace(NOISE, ' ')\n    .split(/\\s+/).filter(Boolean).join(' ');\n}\n```\n\nIt strips `ONSHORE`, `OFFSHORE` and `EXTENSION` — the exact words that distinguish physically\ndifferent assets. Applied to the 921 NESO site names:\n\n```\ndistinct keys after normalisation   886\nkeys claimed by 2+ different sites   34\nsites inside a colliding key         69      (7.5% of the network)\n\nMORAY EAST     <- MORAY EAST ONSHORE | MORAY EAST ONSHORE | MORAY EAST OFFSHORE\nBEATRICE       <- BEATRICE ONSHORE   | BEATRICE OFFSHORE\nARECLEOCH      <- ARECLEOCH          | ARECLEOCH EXTENSION\nBURBO BANK     <- BURBO BANK EXTENSION ONSHORE | BURBO BANK EXTENSION OFFSHORE\nDOGGER BANK A  <- DOGGER BANK A ONSHORE | DOGGER BANK A OFFSHORE\n```\n\nAnd the map keeps only the first: `if (key && !byName.has(key)) byName.set(key, point);`\n\nAn onshore and an offshore converter station are different assets, at different voltages, often\ntens of kilometres apart. For those 69 sites the panel binds to whichever loaded first.\n\n**Corroborated independently.** The routing study (`05`) found 5 cable circuits whose straight-line\ndistance exceeds their published built length — physically impossible. The worst publishes\n**0.33 km against a 24.78 km straight line**. That is this defect surfacing in a second dataset.\n\nThis is the same class Codex already fixed once: *\"WBUR's exact-name join binds a different\nWest Burton 96.42 km from the project.\"* Fixed for that instance, not f
